paper_sections.title: Valence-Dependent Coupling of Prefrontal-Amygdala Effective Connectivity during Facial Affect Processing

description.value: The study investigated how positive, negative, and neutral facial affect modulate effective connectivity within a right prefrontal-amygdala-fusiform face area network during dynamic facial affect processing.

design.value: Thirty-three healthy volunteers completed a 6-min functional MRI dynamic face-matching and shape-matching task with alternating blocks. Whole-brain GLM analyses assessed face-versus-shape processing and valence effects, followed by dynamic causal modeling, random-effects family-wise Bayesian model selection, and Bayesian model averaging of a four-region right-hemisphere network.

recruitment_method.value: A group of 33 healthy volunteers was recruited for this study.

medical_condition.value: Healthy volunteers; no subject reported any past or current psychiatric disorder.

task_description.value: All participants completed a 6-min fMRI dynamic face-matching and shape-matching task. Face-matching and shape-matching blocks had a length of 20 s and were presented alternatingly. Each of the 12 blocks, six face and six shape blocks, consisted of five trials with a length of 4 s.

instructions.value: Subjects were instructed to match either the left or the right static item at the bottom with the dynamic item on top and to press either the left or the right button with their dominant hand on a response-pad to indicate their choice as soon as they recognized which probe matched.

stimuli.value: Participants were presented with a dynamic target item and two static probe images below it, one of which matched with the target item with regard to shape or facial expression. Face images came from the Radboud face database and included happy, surprised, neutral, sad, and disgusted facial expressions. Target faces were morphed from 0% neutral to 100% emotional intensity within 4 s; neutral dynamic targets were morphed to surprised emotion from 0% to 30% intensity and back to 0%. Shape targets were morphed from a round circle into polygons with three to eight vertices.

description.value: Functional images were acquired with a multiband echoplanar images (EPIs) sequence: 15° tilted downwards from AC-PC, 54 slices, matrix size 96 × 94 px, flip angle 80°, no gap, SENSE-factor 2, and MB-factor 2. Five dummy scans were acquired before the actual data acquisition to establish steady-state conditions.

model_type.value: Repeated measures ANOVA and paired t tests

model_settings.value: A repeated measures ANOVA tested effects between valence conditions, and paired t tests tested differences in performance between face and shape matching. Trials without response or with RT <100 ms were excluded from the behavioral analysis.

estimator.value: Repeated measures ANOVA and paired t tests

model_settings.value: The first-level analysis modeled the individual onset and length of each 4-s trial for face-matching and shape-matching. The final whole-brain GLM included regressors for all faces, positive faces, negative faces, neutral faces, and shapes, plus six realignment parameters as nuisance regressors. The main task effect was tested with a one-sample t test using subject contrast files, and valence was tested with a second-level repeated measures ANOVA.

A four-region right-hemisphere network comprising the ventrolateral LPFC, MPFC, AMY, and FFA was modeled. Bidirectional intrinsic connections were specified between MPFC and AMY, MPFC and LPFC, FFA and LPFC, and FFA and AMY; all possible intrinsic connectivity patterns between LPFC and AMY were included. Positive and negative valence modulation was varied across MPFC–LPFC and MPFC–AMY connections, producing 256 models. The all-faces regressor was the driving input to the FFA.

Four model families were compared: no contextual valence modulations (one model), bottom-up modulations (15 models), top-down modulations (15 models), and bidirectional modulations (225 models). Expected posterior probabilities and exceedance probabilities were computed.

estimator.value: Random-effects family-wise Bayesian model selection using free energy as a lower-bound approximation to log-model evidence

model_settings.value: Parameters were averaged across models of the winning bidirectional family and weighted by posterior model probability to account for uncertainty in individual models.

model_settings.value: One-sample t tests of Bayesian-model-averaged endogenous and modulatory parameter estimates were conducted across subjects. Multiple connectivity-parameter tests were corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate at adjusted p FDRc < 0.05.

estimator.value: One-sample t tests with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction

description.value: The all-faces regressor included all 30 face events from the six face-matching blocks.
Two positively valenced blocks included happy, surprised, and neutral faces. Each trial contained at least one happy face, and the average face valence was 3.55 ± 0.08.
Two negatively valenced blocks used sad and disgusted faces instead of fearful faces; the average face valence was 2.01 ± 0.04.

Two neutrally valenced blocks used neutral and surprised faces; neutral dynamic targets were morphed to surprised emotion from 0% to 30% intensity and back to 0%. The average face valence was 2.94 ± 0.04.
Six shape-matching blocks used shapes superimposed on a whirled face. The target shape was morphed from a round circle into a polygon with three to eight vertices.

interpretations.value: The dynamic face-matching and shape-matching task showed a significant effect of task in brain regions commonly recruited during face processing.
